newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - FEB 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - FEB 3.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The general price index has marked an impressive increase of 25.47 percent since the beginning the year, the best performance investors have seen since 1994. Investment capital has surpassed the seven trillion drachma mark and is calculated at 24.37 of GDP for 1996, figures not seen since 1990.
--Smaller banks have been the big winners in the returns from bonds and foreign exchange, reaching levels forecast for the whole of 1997 in the first month of the year.
--The National Bank is planning a new rescheduling of debts on favourable terms: sources say the rescheduling will be for loans taken out before 1995.

--The secrets of the Bank of Greece's exchange policy are read in statements by the governor on Friday: the drachma will be stable but not necessarily against the Ecu. This siginificant change in monetary policy is hidden in small differentiation in the usual language used by the governor, who referred to "exchange parities against the currencies which make up the European Currency Unit", rather than the Ecu itself.
--The 80s property boom, which saw prices rise by 400-500 percent in Athens' northern suburbs in the latter half of the deacde, is winding down with homebuyers now returning to the city centre.

--The government will make significant inroads in the shipping, insurance, market regulation and farm sectors soon, with the aim of forging major changes by the end of the year. Coordination of the effort has been undertaken by National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou, on the express orders of Prime Minister Costas Simitis.

--The administration of the Commercial Bank is trying to carefully overcome problems in its latest budget, which has shown that there are more department heads than employees. Meanwhile, scenarios for the future of the Ionian bank are back in the spotlight with pressure for its sale increasing.

--Major league football teams have recorded a cumulative record loss of 17.5 billion drachmas, due to exorbitant contracts with players, a dramatic dowtown in revenues from fans at the gates and bad management.

--A document from the development ministry reveals that it there are no unexpected developments in the market, the prices of basic goods will fall by 10.0 percent. Few items, the ministry believes, will rise above 5.0 percent.

--There are good returns lying in store for mutual funds placements, following the fall of interest rates. The active capital for mutual funds has already increased by 12.0 percent since the beginning of the year.
--Titan Cement is flirting with the Bulgarians, making a bid to buyout a local cement industry. It will face-off with multinational construction heavies such as Holderbank and Lafarge.
